extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Tatler / early-18th-century literate public interested in essays, criticism, and news
extracted.subtask_description: Short periodical essays and newsy miscellanies in the style of Steele's The Tatler: light literary criticism, social commentary, and anecdotal news written in common speech with moral aims. Emphasizes tone, judgment, and selective liberties in reporting/reinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatrical entertainment should engage the understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: “The stage being an entertainment of the reason and all our faculties, this way of being pleased with the suspense of them for three hours together... seems to arise rather from the degeneracy of our understanding, than an improvement of our diversions.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticizes entertainments (here, the Italian opera) that please only the senses (eyes and ears) while excluding intellectual engagement. Example: complaint that a large part of a performance in Italian left the understanding no part in the pleasure and provoked a critic to write against operas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language intelligibility and contextual consistency in performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Concern that performances mix languages, times, and places so as to confuse audience understanding: a great part of the performance being done in Italian produced criticism that 'time and place, but languages and nations [were] confused.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mixing foreign language segments or incongruent historical/geographic elements can alienate or infuriate critics and reduce the work's intellectual credibility. The passage uses the opera example to show how such confusion harms reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portraiture (painting) should reflect sitter's character and social effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that Mr. Jervas painted Clarissa 'in a manner that looks artless, and innocent of the torments she gives'; Chloe is 'drawn with a liveliness that shows she is conscious, but not affected, of her perfections.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The painter's choices (pose, dress — e.g. Chloe's straw hat and riband) should convey the sitter's nature and the kind of effect their beauty has on others (familiarity vs artlessness). The example argues for matching visual representation to psychological/social character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convey different types of beauty by their effects on admirers
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction: 'Clarissa never fails of gaining admiration; Chloe, of moving desire.' The different beauties are 'suitably represented' and produce different behaviors among lovers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When characterizing persons (in portrait, prose, or drama), show the social/psychological impact of their qualities — e.g., one beauty provokes melancholy admiration, another immediate transport and gaiety (leading to coxcombs versus madmen). Use observed effects to dramatize differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic thought should be just and natural
rubrics_metrics.description: Praise that 'All Milton's thoughts are wonderfully just and natural' in his description; friction when another poet uses similar imagery in a different context (Dryden's verse) may be less appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate poetry for naturalness and appropriateness of thought and image to speaker/context. The passage contrasts Milton (natural, fitting) with Dryden (similar image in a different, arguably less fitting, context).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use epithets judiciously in epic poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of Homer's frequent epithets (e.g., Πόδας ὠχὺς ‘swift-footed’) being used in contexts where speed is irrelevant; Virgil is praised as more judicious in choosing epithets appropriate to action and character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid repetitive or mechanically-applied epithets that jar with the described action; choose epithets that remain appropriate in varied narrative situations. Example: Virgil drops 'pius' or 'pater' where it would be absurd in a given scene (e.g., Dido's cave).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pamphlet/essay tone: clarity, lively manner, and restrained passion
rubrics_metrics.description: On a 'Project for the Advancement of Religion' the writer praises its 'clear and lively manner, without unseasonable passions; and the whole air of the book, as to the language, the sentiments, and the reasonings, show it was written by one whose virtue sits easy about him.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective religious/political/personal pamphlets should be lucid, spirited, and free from inappropriate emotional excess. Language, sentiment, and argument should convey steadiness of character and moral seriousness rather than rant or excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tatler-style reporting: liberty to reinterpret old material within stylistic limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorial rule: 'I shall always take the liberty to tell for news such things (let them have happened never so much before the time of writing) as have escaped public notice... provided that I am still within rules, and trespass not as a Tatler any further than in an incorrectness of style, and writing in an air of common speech.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allows repackaging or re-presenting older events as 'news' if they illuminate character or inspire admiration; stylistic informality and common-speech are acceptable, but one must respect the paper's other rules and limits (moral/legal/procedural).

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge wit by evidence of judgment rather than accidental cleverness
rubrics_metrics.description: On Sappho: much of her behaviour suggests 'all her wit is mere good luck, and not the effect of reason and judgment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a writer or conversationalist, distinguish between wit that stems from deliberate insight and that which appears random or lucky; prefer and praise wit showing judgment and design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public writing should condemn vice and immoral stage content
rubrics_metrics.description: Footnote commentary: the pamphlet is 'closely in accord with the Tatler in its condemnation of gaming, drunkenness, swearing, immorality on the stage, and other evils of the time.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As an ethical/critical standard, reviewers and moralists of the period (and this author) countenance public censure of entertainments and practices that promote vice; prefer works and performances that avoid corrupting influences.
